To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

a social-preference cycle of any sort can be produced in any society by a voting system that satisfies three conditions: (1) it is anonymous, (2) it is neutral, and (3) it has the single-winner property.
a cycle of any kind and a dominant cycle are both possible only if a certain condition is satisfied, and that this condition is satisfied if and only if the voting system is not majority rule.

a) the Voting Paradox can be generalized to a necessary and sufficient condition for cyclic social preference; b) this condition is as general as any possible condition for cyclic social choice; and c) the condition is a relaxation of majority decision, and is therefore not peculiar to majority decision.
In summary, our research is concerned with

a class of problems which can be formulated in the following way: Given a set of n elements, a set of m binary relations on this set, and a subset A of the n elements, determine whether there is a permutation of the set of n elements such that each of the m binary relations can be represented by a permutation matrix.
the problem of the rationality of the choice between two alternatives by a group of agents.
the following questions. What is the relationship between the structure of social preference cycles and the structure of the underlying voting system?
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
a cycle of any type, or a cycle of a specific type (dominance) is possible if and only if the voting rule fails to meet the condition of “cyclical consistency.”
, given the assumptions of the sufficiency theorem, the only way to avoid a cycle is to avoid a relaxation of majority, and the only way to guarantee a cycle is to guarantee a relaxation of majority.
a cycle in the preference profile of any social choice procedure is necessary and sufficient for a cycle in the profile of majority rule.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the cycle is a procedural condition necessary and (under the given assumptions) sufficient for cyclic social choice.

, if a social preference relation is to be cyclic, it is not only sufficient but also necessary that there exist a set of individuals such that each of them has a different strict preference over the set.
, if the social-preference cycle is a possibility, then it is a possibility for any voting rule that satisfies the “Latin square” condition.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the existence of a cycle in social preference is an inevitable byproduct of the fact that the preferences of individuals are not always the same.
, if social preferences are to be cyclic, then the social preference function must be cyclic.
, in the presence of a certain sort of diversity in individual preference, a social preference is likely to be cyclic.
